title: Manufacturing Processes
description: A survey and applied design course covering major manufacturing processes, materials-process relationships, process planning, CNC/CAD/CAM, metrology, quality control, economics, sustainability, and design for manufacturability.

topics.title: Manufacturing Strategy, Materials, and Process Selection
topics.description: This opening topic frames manufacturing as an engineering decision system: the right process depends on function, material behavior, tolerances, quantity, cost, and lifecycle priorities.

children.title: Manufacturing process families
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn the map of manufacturing so later details fit into a usable decision framework.

children.title: Primary shaping, forming, subtractive, joining, surface processing, additive, and assembly
Process capability windows: geometry, material, tolerance, throughput, and cost
Product lifecycle stages from prototype to production ramp
Engineering materials for manufacturing
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to connect material properties to what can realistically be made.

children.title: Metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, and powders
Strength, ductility, hardness, melting behavior, thermal properties, and machinability
Processing-structure-property relationships
Process selection logic
children.description: Why it matters: Students practice choosing processes by balancing constraints rather than memorizing isolated methods.

children.title: Part function, material compatibility, geometry, tolerance, surface finish, and production volume
Make-buy decisions, supplier capability, and equipment availability
Tradeoffs among performance, cost, speed, quality, and sustainability

topics.title: Casting, Molding, and Primary Shaping Processes
topics.description: Casting and molding introduce how liquid or softened material becomes a finished or near-net-shape part, making this topic central for metals, polymers, and high-volume production.

children.title: Foundry fundamentals
children.description: Why it matters: Students see how molten metal handling, solidification, and tooling shape final quality.

children.title: Patterns, molds, cores, gating, risers, shrinkage, and feeding
Sand casting, investment casting, die casting, and permanent mold casting
Solidification defects, porosity, inclusions, and hot tears
Polymer molding foundations
children.description: Why it matters: The point is to understand why plastic part design depends so strongly on tooling and flow.

children.title: Injection molding, compression molding, blow molding, thermoforming, and extrusion molding
Flow length, cooling, shrinkage, warpage, draft, ribs, bosses, and sink marks
Thermoplastics versus thermosets
Casting and molding design rules
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to design parts that a real shop can produce consistently.

children.title: Parting lines, draft angles, wall thickness, corner radii, and ejection
Tooling cost and volume economics
Inspection needs for internal and surface defects

topics.title: Bulk Deformation: Forging, Rolling, Extrusion, and Drawing
topics.description: Bulk deformation processes reshape material through plastic flow, so the emphasis is on force, temperature, tooling, grain flow, and property changes.

children.title: Deformation mechanics
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn why plastic deformation can improve strength but also create defects if poorly controlled.

children.title: Stress-strain behavior beyond yield
Cold, warm, and hot working
Work hardening, recrystallization, anisotropy, and grain flow
Major bulk forming processes
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to distinguish process capabilities and when each process is economically appropriate.

children.title: Forging, rolling, extrusion, wire drawing, bar drawing, and swaging
Open-die versus closed-die tooling
Load, friction, lubrication, temperature, and die wear
Forming defects and quality
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn the failure modes that limit manufacturability.

children.title: Cracks, laps, seams, residual stresses, center burst, and dimensional variation
Process maps, forming limits, and lubrication control
Inspection and post-forming heat treatment

topics.title: Sheet Metal Forming and Pressworking
topics.description: Sheet forming covers the processes used for enclosures, vehicle bodies, appliances, brackets, and stamped components where thin material must hold precise shape.

children.title: Sheet forming operations
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn the standard operations behind high-volume metal parts.

children.title: Shearing, blanking, punching, bending, deep drawing, stretching, and roll forming
Presses, dies, punches, blank holders, and progressive tooling
Springback, bend allowance, bend radius, and neutral axis
Formability and failure
children.description: Why it matters: The point is to predict when sheet material can stretch or draw without tearing or wrinkling.

children.title: Forming-limit diagrams
Wrinkling, tearing, earing, thinning, and residual stress
Material anisotropy and lubrication
Design for stamped parts
children.description: Why it matters: Students connect part design choices to tooling complexity and production yield.

children.title: Hole-to-edge spacing, bend relief, corner radii, and consistent wall features
Tooling cost, nesting, scrap, and production volume
Tolerance stack-up and secondary operations

topics.title: Machining Fundamentals and Cutting Processes
topics.description: Machining is the core subtractive process family; students learn how tools remove material while controlling accuracy, surface finish, tool life, and cost.

children.title: Cutting mechanics
children.description: Why it matters: This subtopic explains what happens at the tool-chip interface and why cutting conditions matter.

children.title: Chip formation, shear plane, built-up edge, cutting forces, and power
Tool materials, coatings, rake angle, clearance angle, and wear
Speed, feed, depth of cut, material removal rate, and tool life
Common machining operations
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn what each machine tool does and which geometries it produces well.

children.title: Turning, facing, boring, drilling, reaming, tapping, milling, broaching, sawing, and shaping
Workholding, fixturing, datums, and setup planning
Manual versus CNC machine tools
Machining economics and quality
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to make process plans that meet tolerance without wasting time or tooling.

children.title: Cycle time, setup time, tool change time, and batch size
Surface finish, dimensional accuracy, burrs, chatter, and heat effects
Roughing and finishing strategy

topics.title: Abrasive Machining, Finishing, and Surface Treatments
topics.description: Finishing processes determine final accuracy, surface integrity, wear behavior, and appearance, especially when conventional machining cannot deliver required tolerances.

children.title: Abrasive processes
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn how small cutting grains create precision surfaces.

children.title: Grinding, honing, lapping, polishing, abrasive blasting, and superfinishing
Wheel selection, grit size, bond type, dressing, and coolant
Burn, residual stress, and surface damage
Surface engineering
children.description: Why it matters: This subtopic shows how surfaces can be modified without changing the bulk material.

children.title: Heat treatment, carburizing, nitriding, shot peening, anodizing, plating, coating, and painting
Hardness, corrosion resistance, fatigue strength, friction, and wear
Adhesion, coating thickness, and environmental controls
Surface measurement
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to specify and verify surface quality with engineering language.

children.title: Roughness parameters such as Ra and Rz
Surface texture symbols and drawing notes
Profilometry, visual standards, and functional surface requirements

topics.title: Joining, Welding, Fastening, and Assembly
topics.description: Joining processes turn individual parts into products, so this topic connects material compatibility, heat effects, joint design, inspection, and assembly efficiency.

children.title: Welding and thermal joining
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn the main fusion and solid-state joining processes and their risks.

children.title: Arc welding, resistance welding, laser welding, brazing, soldering, friction welding, and ultrasonic welding
Heat-affected zones, distortion, residual stress, and metallurgical changes
Weld symbols, joint preparation, filler metals, shielding, and process variables
Mechanical fastening and adhesives
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to compare joining options when welding is impractical or undesirable.

children.title: Bolts, screws, rivets, clips, inserts, snap fits, and press fits
Adhesive bonding, surface preparation, cure conditions, and joint loading
Disassembly, maintenance, vibration, corrosion, and mixed-material assemblies
Assembly process design
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to reduce cost and defects through product and fixture design.

children.title: Design for assembly principles
Poka-yoke, fixtures, jigs, sequence planning, and ergonomic assembly
Inspection points and rework loops

topics.title: Polymer, Composite, Ceramic, and Powder Processing
topics.description: This topic extends manufacturing beyond conventional metals, emphasizing how material class changes processing constraints, tooling, defects, and applications.

children.title: Polymer processing
children.description: Why it matters: Students connect polymer behavior to everyday manufacturing methods.

children.title: Extrusion, injection molding, blow molding, thermoforming, compression molding, and rotational molding
Viscosity, temperature, cooling rate, shrinkage, and warpage
Recycling, additives, fillers, and design for molded plastics
Composite and ceramic processing
children.description: Why it matters: The point is to understand why brittle and anisotropic materials demand different process controls.

children.title: Layup, filament winding, resin transfer molding, pultrusion, autoclave curing, slip casting, pressing, and sintering
Fiber orientation, resin content, voids, delamination, and cure cycles
Ceramic shrinkage, green strength, densification, and thermal shock
Powder metallurgy
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn how parts can be built from powders when melting or machining is inefficient.

children.title: Powder production, blending, compaction, sintering, infiltration, and hot isostatic pressing
Porosity, density, particle size, and dimensional change
Bearings, gears, filters, cutting tools, and near-net-shape parts

topics.title: Additive Manufacturing and Rapid Prototyping
topics.description: Additive manufacturing is treated as both a prototyping tool and a production process family with its own design rules, materials, economics, and qualification challenges.

children.title: Additive process categories
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn the major AM technologies and what each can make well.

children.title: Material extrusion, vat photopolymerization, powder bed fusion, binder jetting, directed energy deposition, sheet lamination, and material jetting
Metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, and support materials
Build orientation, supports, layer thickness, infill, and post-processing
Design for additive manufacturing
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to exploit AM advantages without ignoring process limits.

children.title: Topology optimization, lattice structures, consolidation, internal channels, and mass customization
Overhangs, anisotropy, tolerance, surface finish, and minimum feature size
Support removal, heat treatment, machining allowance, and finishing
Qualification and production use
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn why printing a part is different from certifying a repeatable process.

children.title: Process monitoring, material traceability, build records, and inspection
Cost models for prototype, bridge, and production quantities
Failure modes, standards, and acceptance testing

topics.title: CNC, CAD/CAM, Automation, and Smart Manufacturing
topics.description: Modern manufacturing depends on digital instructions, automated equipment, connected data, and feedback control, making this topic the bridge from individual processes to production systems.

children.title: CNC programming and CAM workflow
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn how digital geometry becomes machine motion.

children.title: CAD models, setup sheets, tool libraries, toolpaths, post-processors, and G-code
Work coordinate systems, feeds and speeds, cutter compensation, and simulation
Collision checking, verification, and first-article approval
Automation and production equipment
children.description: Why it matters: The point is to understand how automation changes capability, safety, consistency, and cost.

children.title: Robots, conveyors, automated inspection, pallet changers, feeders, and flexible manufacturing cells
Sensors, actuators, PLCs, machine vision, and industrial safety
Changeover, uptime, maintenance, and human-machine collaboration
Smart manufacturing data
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to use manufacturing data for monitoring and improvement.

children.title: Digital twins, MES, SCADA, IIoT, machine connectivity, and data standards
OEE, downtime tracking, process dashboards, and alarms
Cybersecurity and data integrity in connected factories

topics.title: Process Planning, Routing, Tooling, and Production Ramp
topics.description: Process planning turns a design into an executable manufacturing route, so students practice sequencing operations, selecting tooling, estimating capacity, and preparing for scale-up.

children.title: Routing and operation planning
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to write a practical route sheet for a part.

children.title: Operation sequence, setup strategy, datum transfer, work instructions, and inspection hold points
Machine selection, fixture selection, tool selection, and outsourcing decisions
Process sheets, travelers, bills of materials, and revision control
Tooling and fixtures
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to see tooling as a major driver of accuracy, speed, repeatability, and cost.

children.title: Jigs, fixtures, dies, molds, cutting tools, gauges, and custom workholding
Tool life, maintainability, spare tooling, and setup reduction
Capital cost versus per-part cost
Prototype to production ramp
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn why processes that work once must be stabilized before scale.

children.title: Pilot builds, first articles, capability studies, and production readiness reviews
Supplier qualification, documentation, training, and control plans
Ramp risks: yield loss, bottlenecks, changeovers, and late design changes

topics.title: Metrology, Tolerancing, Process Capability, and Quality Control
topics.description: Manufacturing quality requires measurable specifications, capable processes, and feedback systems that detect variation before it becomes field failure.

children.title: Measurement systems and metrology
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn how to verify parts with appropriate instruments and uncertainty awareness.

children.title: Calipers, micrometers, height gauges, CMMs, optical comparators, gauges, and scanners
Accuracy, precision, resolution, repeatability, reproducibility, calibration, and traceability
Gauge R&R and measurement system analysis
Tolerancing and GD&T foundations
children.description: Why it matters: The point is to communicate manufacturable requirements clearly.

children.title: Datums, basic dimensions, position, flatness, parallelism, perpendicularity, runout, and profile
Tolerance stack-up and functional dimensioning
Drawing interpretation and inspection planning
Statistical quality and capability
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to separate normal variation from process trouble.

children.title: Control charts, process capability indices Cp and Cpk, sampling plans, and acceptance criteria
Pareto charts, root cause analysis, corrective action, and continuous improvement
Scrap, rework, yield, and cost of poor quality

topics.title: Design for Manufacturing, Assembly, Cost, and Sustainability
topics.description: This topic asks students to redesign parts and products so they are easier to make, assemble, inspect, repair, and recycle.

children.title: Design for manufacturability
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to spot features that drive unnecessary manufacturing difficulty.

children.title: Feature simplification, standard stock sizes, minimum radii, wall thickness, tolerance relaxation, and material substitution
Process-specific design rules for casting, molding, machining, sheet metal, welding, and additive manufacturing
Design reviews with manufacturing engineers and suppliers
Manufacturing economics
children.description: Why it matters: The goal is to estimate cost drivers well enough to compare alternatives.

children.title: Fixed cost, variable cost, tooling cost, labor, cycle time, material utilization, scrap, overhead, and learning curves
Break-even analysis and quantity-sensitive process choice
Cost of quality, inspection cost, and inventory implications
Sustainable and circular manufacturing
children.description: Why it matters: Students learn to include environmental and lifecycle concerns in process decisions.

children.title: Energy use, material yield, emissions, coolant, waste, and hazardous substances
Design for repair, remanufacturing, recycling, and disassembly
Lifecycle assessment basics and circular manufacturing strategies

topics.title: Integrated Manufacturing Case Study and Process Plan
topics.description: The final topic integrates course knowledge into a realistic engineering deliverable: select a part, choose processes, justify tradeoffs, and document a defensible production plan.

children.title: Part and requirement analysis
children.description: Why it matters: Students start by translating a product need into manufacturing requirements.

children.title: Function, loads, environment, materials, geometry, tolerances, finish, regulatory needs, and volume
Critical-to-quality characteristics
Assumptions, constraints, and risk register
Process comparison and justification
children.description: Why it matters: The point is to make a reasoned recommendation rather than a list of options.

children.title: Candidate process matrix
Cost, quality, capability, lead time, equipment, supplier, and sustainability tradeoffs
Prototype, low-volume, and high-volume alternatives
Final manufacturing plan
children.description: Why it matters: Students produce a concise plan that resembles professional manufacturing documentation.

children.title: Routing, tooling, fixtures, inspection plan, quality controls, and production ramp steps
Manufacturing economics and break-even estimate
Presentation of decisions, risks, and next experiments
